arXiv:2605.14071v1 [cs.CL] 13 May 2026

Distribution Corrected Offline Data Distillation for Large Language Models

Yumeng Zhang    Zhengbang Yang    Yevin Nikhel Goonatilake    Zhuangdi Zhu Affiliation: George Mason University, Fairfax, VA, USA
Abstract

Distilling reasoning traces from strong large language models into smaller ones is a promising route to improve intelligence in resource-constrained settings. Existing approaches face a fundamental trade-off: offline distillation from teacher-generated traces provides high-quality, sample-efficient supervision but suffers from distributional drift: during training, the student model conditions on teacher-generated prefixes, whereas during inference the student autoregresses on self-generated prefixes, leading to compounding errors over long reasoning trajectories. Meanwhile, on-policy or self-distillation methods better match the student’s inference-time distribution, but require costly online sampling and often produce low-quality traces in early training. We propose a principled offline reasoning distillation framework that preserves the efficiency and supervision quality of offline teacher-generated data while correcting teacher–student distribution drift. It adaptively emphasizes teacher supervision that is better aligned with the student’s on-policy distribution. Evaluations on mathematical reasoning benchmarks of GSM8K, MATH, MATH500, and harder held-out competition-style tasks, including AMC, AIME, and OlympiadBench, show that our method improves reasoning accuracy over prior offline distillation algorithms and yields more stable reasoning traces while preserving instruction-following capabilities. Our work shows that lightweight, distribution-correction-aware training can substantially strengthen offline reasoning distillation without online rollouts.11 1 Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Discord-E6BC.

1 Introduction

Reasoning ability has emerged as a cornerstone of modern large language models (LLMs), largely driven by scaled model architecture and advances in reinforcement learning (RL)-based post-training optimization. This capability is particularly important in scientific and engineering domains such as mathematics, robotics, and physics, where solving problems requires structured, multi-step reasoning instead of short-horizon token prediction. Despite these advances, high-quality reasoning behavior is still primarily observed in large or proprietary models. Enabling smaller models to acquire similar reasoning ability is critical for practical deployment, especially in resource-constrained environments where efficient and reliable intelligence is required. The ability to transfer reasoning competence across models without significant performance degradation is crucial.

A common approach to reasoning distillation is to train a smaller student model on reasoning traces generated by a stronger teacher model. In this paradigm, referred to as offline learning or behavior cloning, training data are collected from an external model. In contrast, on-policy methods generate data from the target model itself and update the model using policy-gradient RL techniques such as GRPO [30] or token-level extensions [21, 42, 46, 43].

Offline distillation offers several advantages. It is typically more sample-efficient, and teacher-generated trajectories provide higher-quality supervision, especially during early stages of training. However, it also faces the inherent limitation of distribution drift: the distribution of teacher-generated trajectories differs from the distribution induced by the student model during inference. As the student generates intermediate tokens that deviate from teacher trajectories, it enters support regions that are underrepresented in the training data. This distribution shift leads to compounding errors and unreliable behavior. Existing approaches alleviate this issue through refined distillation objectives, such as bidirectional divergence minimization [17], but these methods do not directly resolve the distribution mismatch, where the optimization is still focused on a teacher-provided distribution.

We propose a principled method for LLM reasoning distillation that relies solely on offline, teacher-provided data while reducing the distribution gap to on-policy training. We first design a general reasoning-eliciting instruction that contextualizes a large teacher model to produce high-quality reasoning traces. These traces serve as supervision for training a smaller student model. We then introduce a distribution-corrected objective that incorporates an advantage-based weighting mechanism, enabling the student to better align with trajectories it is likely to encounter during inference. Our formulation provides an effective approach for reducing the teacher–student distributional drift and is compatible with most offline distillation frameworks. We focus on mathematical reasoning as a representative domain. Empirical results across multiple models and math benchmarks demonstrate that our method consistently improves the reasoning performance of student models in both in-domain and out-of-domain settings, outperforming existing offline distillation baselines and narrowing the gap to that of online sampling methods without requiring online interaction.

2 Preliminary

On-policy Learning.

On-policy methods, especially on-policy RL, have been widely adopted for LLM post-training in domains such as math reasoning and safety alignment. The core idea behind this approach is to fine-tune a pretrained model πθ\pi_{\theta} to maximize accumulated rewards within a domain 𝒬\mathcal{Q} over self-generated trajectories:

JRL(θ)=𝔼x∼𝒬,y∼πθ(⋅∣x)[ℝ(y,x)],J_{\text{RL}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{Q},\;y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}\left[\mathds{R}(y,x)\right], (1)

where ℝ⁡(x,y)\mathds{R}(x,y) is a reward function that scores a response yy (e.g., a reasoning trajectory). Following the policy gradient principle [32], we derive the following gradient update for Eq. (1):

∇θJRL(θ)=𝔼x∼𝒬,y∼πθ(⋅∣x)⏟On-policy sampling[ℝ(x,y)⋅∑t=0|y|logπθ(yt∣x,y:<t)],\nabla_{\theta}J_{\text{RL}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{Q},\;\underbrace{y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}_{\text{On-policy sampling}}}\left[\mathds{R}(x,y)\cdot\sum_{t=0}^{|y|}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x,\,y_{:<t})\right], (2)

Prior work has improved training stability by replacing the reward function ℝ⁡(x,y)\mathds{R}(x,y) with a normalized Advantage function, tokenizing the optimization formulation, and introducing clipping and model update constraints [30, 7, 21, 42, 46, 43].

A key advantage of this strategy over supervised fine-tuning (SFT) lies in its on-policy learning: the data used to optimize the target model is sampled from itself instead of from another behavior policy. It mitigates distribution drift, where the model encounters underrepresented regions at inference time, and often benefits out-of-domain generalization.

However, online methods are costly in terms of sample collection and labeling, requiring a notably higher number of training samples than supervised fine-tuning, and each trajectory requires labeled rewards. Additionally, for smaller LLMs, the sample quality is also limited by the model’s own capability, which leads to rare high-return trajectories and slow asymptotic convergence.

Offline Knowledge Distillation.

A parallel path towards improving pretrained LLM performance is knowledge distillation from another stronger model, such as an advanced teacher LLM πT\pi_{T}. One straightforward method is to directly perform SFT on teacher-generated reasoning traces, which trains the target (student) model πθ\pi_{\theta} to imitate teacher behavior by maximizing the log-likelihood of teacher-generated responses:

JSFT(θ)=𝔼x∼𝒬,y∼πT(⋅∣x)⏟off-line sampling[∑t=0|y|logπθ(yt∣x,y:<t)].J_{\text{SFT}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{Q},\;\underbrace{y\sim\pi_{T}(\cdot\mid x)}_{\text{off-line sampling}}}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{|y|}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x,\,y_{:<t})\right]. (3)

Here the expectation is taken under the teacher distribution πT\pi_{T}, with yy drawn from an offline dataset provided by the teacher model. This behavior-cloning style method is training- and sampling-efficient but is also prone to performance drop induced by distribution drift, since this offline objective does not directly optimize the target (πθ\pi_{\theta}) model’s performance when yy is sampled from πθ\pi_{\theta} during inference.

Subsequent methods supervise the student model with more refined teacher signals, often by minimizing a distributional divergence between the teacher and student models, such as the KL-divergence:

JKD(θ)=𝔼x∼𝒬,y∼πT(⋅∣x)[𝒟KL(πT(y|x)|πθ(y|x))].\displaystyle J_{\text{KD}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{Q},\;y\sim\pi_{T}(\cdot\mid x)}\left[\mathcal{D}_{\text{KL}}(\pi_{T}(y|x)|\pi_{\theta}(y|x))\right]. (4)

Works along this line include optimizing on a reverse KL divergence 𝒟KL(πθ∥πT)\mathcal{D}_{\text{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{T}) [4] or a mixture of both directions [17]. While these algorithms show empirical performance improvement over direct SFT, they still inherit a fundamental limitation of offline data: the training objective provides a biased signal for the student’s on-policy behavior. At inference time, the student model may generate prefixes that are underrepresented in the offline teacher data, leading to unreliable behavior [1].

3 Methodology: Distribution Corrected Distillation from Offline Data

In this paper, we aim to improve cross-model knowledge distillation for reasoning, where a teacher LLM with more advanced reasoning ability provides supervision for a student LLM. To elicit strong teacher behavior, we first design a reasoning instruction as a conditional context cc when sampling traces from the teacher: y∼πT​(x,c)y\sim\pi_{T}(x;c), which forms an offline reasoning dataset for student distillation.

Our goal is to retain the data-efficiency benefits of offline distillation while reducing the distributional gap between teacher-generated traces and the student’s on-policy behavior. The core idea is to introduce a student-support-aware correction that reweights a training trajectory {x,y∼πT​(x,c)}\{x,y\sim\pi_{T}(x;c)\} with a density ratio π¯θ​(y∣x)π¯T​(y∣x;c)\frac{\bar{\pi}_{\theta}(y\mid x)}{\bar{\pi}_{T}(y\mid x;c)}, where π¯\bar{\pi} denotes a stop-gradient operation.

Stabilized Transformation.

However, directly applying such a density ratio leads to high training instability, as the density ratio is unbounded and accumulates high variance over long sequences. We address this in two steps. First, to obtain a bounded and monotonic approximation, we apply a sigmoid transformation to the log density ratio: r⁡(y∣x)=σ⁡(τ⋅log⁡π¯θ​(y∣x)π¯T​(y∣x;c)),r(y\mid x)=\sigma\!\left(\tau\cdot\log\frac{\bar{\pi}_{\theta}(y\mid x)}{\bar{\pi}_{T}(y\mid x;c)}\right), with a temperature coefficient τ\tau set to 1 by default. It monotonically preserves the ordering induced by the density ratio while mapping the correction into a bounded range of (0,1)(0,1).

Meanwhile, directly applying r⁡(y∣x)r(y\mid x) as a sequence-level weight still introduces length bias, where longer trajectories can accumulate larger aggregate log-probability differences that inflate their correction weights. To mitigate such length bias and variance, we apply token-level approximation, following a strategy that has also been adopted to stabilize RL training [45]. Specifically, we tokenize the correction by applying it as gradient weighting rtr_{t} for each training token yty_{t} in a trajectory y={yt}t<|y|y=\{y_{t}\}_{t<|y|}. This leads to our final reweighting ratio: rt=σ(τlogπ¯θ(yt∣x;y:<t)π¯T(yt∣x;c;y:<t)).r_{t}=\sigma\left(\tau\log\frac{\bar{\pi}_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x;y_{:<t})}{\bar{\pi}_{T}(y_{t}\mid x;c;y_{:<t})}\right).

This formulation can be readily applied to different offline distillation backbones. We illustrate with SFT as the base objective:

∇θJDisCorD (θ)=𝔼x∼𝒬,y∼πT(⋅∣x;c)[∑t=0|y|σ(τlogπ¯θ(yt∣x;y:<t)πT¯(yt∣x;c;y:<t))⋅∇θlogπθ(yt∣x;y:<t)].\nabla_{\theta}J^{\text{{DisCorD} }}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{Q},\;y\sim\pi_{T}(\cdot\mid x;c)}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{|y|}\sigma(\tau\log\frac{\bar{\pi}_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x;y_{:<t})}{\bar{\pi_{T}}(y_{t}\mid x;c;y_{:<t})})\cdot\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x;y_{:<t})\right]. (5)

We refer to the proposed framework as DisCorD (Distribution-Corrected Distillation), which modulates the influence of teacher-provided data supervision based on the student’s current support. It is also compatible with other offline distillation objectives beyond SFT, such as the KL-based formulation in Eq. (4) by replacing the gradient of SFT with that of KL minimization (Section 5).

Implications of the Token-Level Correction.

The correction weight at token tt takes the form using a default temperature of 1:

rt|τ=1=σ(logπ¯θ(yt∣x;y:<t)π¯T(yt∣x;c;y:<t))=π¯θ(yt∣x;y:<t)π¯θ(yt∣x;y:<t)+π¯T(yt∣x;c;y:<t).\displaystyle r_{t}|_{\tau=1}=\sigma\!\left(\log\frac{\bar{\pi}_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x;y_{:<t})}{\bar{\pi}_{T}(y_{t}\mid x;c;y_{:<t})}\right)=\frac{\bar{\pi}_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x;y_{:<t})}{\bar{\pi}_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x;y_{:<t})+\bar{\pi}_{T}(y_{t}\mid x;c;y_{:<t})}.

It can be interpreted as the posterior probability that token yty_{t} was drawn from the student distribution πθ\pi_{\theta} over the teacher distribution πT\pi_{T}, under a uniform prior over the two models [10]. This also connects to contrastive decoding [19], which was applied at model inference time by amplifying the target model’s log-probabilities relative to a weaker model. In contrast, our formulation applies an analogous principle during training, which uses the student-teacher ratio as a soft reweighting to prioritize learning in regions the student is likely to inhabit at inference time.

We demonstrate in Section 5 that this distribution correction improves distilled model performance beyond the instruction prompting baseline with a carefully designed reasoning template. In contrast, several baseline distillation methods can underperform the base model that is prompted with the same reasoning instruction but without fine-tuning.

4 Related Work

We study offline LLM reasoning distillation that tackles the teacher-student distribution drift on fixed offline training traces. This work resides at the intersection of knowledge distillation, post-training optimization, and mathematical reasoning supervision.

Knowledge Distillation (KD).

Knowledge Distillation was initially proposed for conventional AI models, in which a compact student model learns from a stronger teacher via softened predictive distributions or intermediate representations  [3, 2, 13, 27]. This paradigm has been extended to LLMs, where intermediate rationales beyond final answers can be distilled from a strong teacher to a smaller student  [28, 16, 14, 15]. Early reasoning-distillation studies such as Fine-tune-CoT [14] and Distilling Step-by-Step [15] established the value of teacher-generated rationales as supervision for smaller models. Subsequent work has studied how the quality, format, and composition of teacher traces affect distillation. Other studies have improved teacher-generated traces through rationale selection, filtering, structured explanations, and math-specific data curation [38, 35, 23, 22, 44, 33, 5]. These works motivated the use of high-quality offline teacher-generated reasoning traces. However, most methods still train the student model by imitating fixed teacher trajectories under teacher-conditioned prefix distributions. They therefore leave the training-inference distribution drift relatively underexplored: the student is optimized under teacher prefixes during training, but autoregresses on its own prefixes during inference [1, 9, 18, 17].

LLM Post-Training with On-policy vs. Offline Data.

A closer line of work tackles this distribution shift more directly: Online RL and other self-improvement methods optimize on model-generated trajectories over fixed teacher traces. PPO-style RLHF methods [29, 25] and recent reasoning-oriented RL methods such as GRPO [30, 7] generate rollouts from the target model and update the model using outcome or process rewards. Related online or mixed-policy distillation methods, including GKD [1] and CoTD-PO [24], also use student-conditioned or iteratively generated trajectories to better match inference-time behavior. These methods directly reduce the gap between training and inference distributions, but they require additional online sampling, substantially more training-time tokens, and often encounter low-quality student-generated traces early in training. A complementary line of work focuses on redesigning the distillation directions. MiniLLM [9], DistiLLM [18], and ToDi [17] modify autoregressive knowledge-distillation losses through reverse KL, skewed KL, or token-wise divergence control, to better align training and generation behavior. Methods such as DistiLLM still require online student sampling to minimize the reverse KL divergence. Our method resides in the purely offline setting, but focuses on the correction at a different level: instead of changing the divergence measure, we adaptively reweight teacher-token supervision based on the student–teacher distribution mismatch. In this sense, our method changes how the offline teacher supervision is allocated, thus producing a distribution-corrected training signal while preserving the sample efficiency of fixed teacher traces. Our formulation can be readily combined with SFT and other KL-based divergence measures. Compared with online methods such as GKD and CoTD-PO, our method remains fully offline without requiring student rollouts. Prior offline distillation work, such as ToDi, has mainly been applied to the instruction-following domain; we studied DisCorD’s effect in mathematical reasoning distillation as an empirically more challenging domain (Sec 5.2).

Math Reasoning Supervision and Evaluation.

Mathematical reasoning also motivates fine-grained supervision: uniform imitation treats all teacher tokens equally, even though an early algebraic or logical error can propagate through an entire solution. This has motivated process-level supervision and verifier-style frameworks. Outcome-level verifiers and reward models judge complete solutions or final answers [6, 31], while process-supervised methods provide finer-grained feedback on intermediate reasoning steps [34, 20, 36]. Related correction-based frameworks further use teacher feedback to identify and revise erroneous reasoning traces [41].

Our work is complementary to this literature: we design a chain-of-thought reasoning template to elicit strong reasoning traces from the teacher model without introducing a new verifier or search procedure. We then move beyond uniform token imitation and use mismatch-aware reweighting to emphasize teacher supervision that better aligns with the student-conditioned inference distribution.

5 Experiments

We evaluate our method on mathematical reasoning benchmarks across diverse teacher-student configurations, varying model families, sizes, and tasks, with both in- and out-of-domain assessment and qualitative trace analysis. We provide additional results on more experimental settings in the Appendix C. Our main experiments were organized around four questions:

Q1. Does our offline distillation method improve the student model’s reasoning compared to state-of-the-art offline distillation counterparts (Section 5.2)?

Q2. Is the distillation benefit consistent across different model families (Section 5.3)?

Q3. Does the method actually reduce teacher-student behavior divergence under student-generated prefixes during inference time (Section 5.4)?

Q4. Does the resulting student reasoning performance reflect higher quality in correctness, conciseness, and reliability (Section 5.5)?

Q5. Why do we adopt the proposed transformations for stabilizing the distribution correction weights instead of alternative formulations (Section 5.6)?

5.1 Experimental Setup: Baselines, Metrics, and Evaluation Protocols

Models and Teacher Reasoning Instruction.

We used Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct as teachers [26], with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, and Llama-3.2-3B as students. Teacher traces were generated offline using a structured reasoning prompt (Appendix B) that elicits five stages: problem understanding, strategy selection, solution, verification, and final answer. We retained only traces where the teacher’s final answer is correct for distillation training. The same generation-and-filtering pipeline was used for both MATH and GSM8K training data.

Benchmarks.

For in-domain evaluation, we distill on MATH [12] and GSM8K [6] training splits and evaluate on their corresponding test sets, e.g., using MATH500 [20] for MATH-trained checkpoints. For out-of-domain (OOD) evaluation, models trained on MATH were further tested on OlympiadBench [11]22 2 For OlympiadBench, we evaluated all performance on the non-combinatorics subset as all training corpora contain no combinatorics problems., Omni-Math [8], and AMC23, which do not appear in the training domain.

Baselines.

We compared both fully offline distillation objectives and an online baseline. SFT uses the basic cross-entropy loss on teacher-generated reasoning traces. KL uses KL divergence to measure teacher-student distribution difference on the same offline traces, symmetric KL combines forward KL and reverse KL divergence terms, following the broader line of LLM distillation work that studies forward/reverse KL combinations and bidirectional divergence objectives [17, 40]. ToDi [17] is an offline distillation baseline. GKD [1] is an online method reported for reference that relies on frequent sampling of student-generated traces for training. For objectives where our correction is applicable, including SFT and KL, the DisCorD-augmented variant applies the proposed token-level reweighting to the same fixed teacher traces. See Appendix G for detailed formulation. We also report the base model, the CoT-prompted student, and the CoT-prompted teacher as reference points for interpreting lower-bound, prompting-only, and teacher-level performance.

Evaluation metrics.

Final-answer accuracy (↑\uparrow) is our primary metric computed using a mathematical-equivalence pipeline. Distributional ExAccErr ↓\downarrow: For divergence measurement, we evaluated the additional teacher-student next-token distribution gap induced by conditioning on student-generated prefixes rather than teacher prefixes. The initial definition was proposed in MiniLLM [9]. Appendix H provides the detailed formulation. Reasoning reliability: In Section 5.5, we evaluated whether correct answers produced by our method are supported by stable reasoning quality using both automatic metrics and AI-as-Judge annotations. See Appendix C for more details.

5.2 Reasoning Accuracy Comparison

This subsection evaluates final-answer accuracy along two axes: (i) whether DisCorD improves fully offline teacher-trace distillation compared with prior art, and (ii) how offline distillation methods compare with online training with student-rollouts such as GKD, and how they compare with tuning-free methods using a carefully designed reasoning instruction. The results lead to three main observations:

First, DisCorD yields the most consistent gains on MATH-style reasoning tasks, where solutions typically require longer reasoning traces and prefix drift is more likely to affect generation. As shown in Table 1, on the in-domain MATH500 benchmark, DisCorD improves the corresponding offline objectives in the main Qwen settings. The gains are not limited to standard teacher-CoT SFT: our method also improves the symmetric-KL objective in multiple settings, suggesting that the proposed correction can serve as a flexible reweighting mechanism for different offline distillation losses.

Comparisons with tuning-free prompting further highlight this effect. In the 7B→\rightarrow3B setting, SFT underperforms the instruction-prompted student on MATH500, while DisCorD achieves performance beyond instruction prompting. This indicates that direct behavior cloning on teacher traces may weaken the student’s potential for reasoning elicitation, whereas our method allocates supervision more effectively to teacher tokens that remain compatible with the student’s own generation behavior.

Results on GSM8K are less discriminative, likely because the task requires shorter reasoning traces and is less impacted by prefix distribution drift. Strong baselines already plateau after training on traces generated by our reasoning instruction. For example, in the 7B→\rightarrow3B setting, SFT+DisCorD is slightly below SFT on GSM8K, and symmetric KL+DisCorD is tied with symmetric KL, even though DisCorD improves the corresponding MATH500 results and several OOD benchmarks. We consider GSM8K as a shorter-trace setting where the benefit of distribution correction is less pronounced. This interpretation is consistent with our ablations in Section 5.6 and Appendix A, where different transformations of the correction weight have more pronounced effects on longer MATH-style tasks, whereas GSM8K is less sensitive to a specific correction-weighting design.

Second, the improvements transfer to OOD competition-style benchmarks. In the 7B→\rightarrow3B setting, DisCorD outperforms the corresponding offline objectives on several OOD evaluations, including OlympiadBench, Omni-Math, and AMC23. These results suggest that distribution-corrected distillation improves generalization to related competition-style mathematical reasoning tasks.

Third, our method narrows the gap to online student-rollout distillation. GKD remains stronger on some in-domain and OOD benchmarks, as expected, because it trains on student-conditioned online samples and directly observes the student’s rollout distribution. In contrast, DisCorD uses only fixed teacher traces, yet achieves stronger performance than offline baselines. Concretely, DisCorD generates no student-rollout tokens during training and uses only 3.12 GPU-hours, while GKD generates about 2.86M online student-rollout tokens and requires 49.56 GPU-hours, about 15.9×\times more compute. This suggests that our distribution-corrected distillation can approach the benefits of online training while preserving the sample efficiency of offline learning.

5.3 Robustness Across Model Distillation Settings

We further examined the robustness of different methods under varying teacher-student size configurations and model families. Table 2 reports results using Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct as the teacher and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct or Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct as the student, which are consistent with the main findings: our distribution correction method generally improves offline distillation objectives across both student sizes, and is most beneficial for longer mathematical reasoning traces, where teacher-student prefix mismatch has more room to affect generation. For the 14B→\rightarrow3B setting, SFT+DisCorD improves over SFT on both MATH500 and GSM8K, with gains of 2.20 and 1.52 points, respectively. For the smaller 14B→\rightarrow1.5B setting, the gains are larger on MATH500.

To isolate the effect of the student model family, we also distilled a Llama-3.2-3B student from Qwen2.5 teachers using the same objectives as in the main experiments, and evaluated the resulting models on MATH500. As shown in Table 3, the cross-family results are consistent with the primary findings in Section 5.2: the DisCorD-augmented objectives remain competitive with baselines that minimize teacher-student logit divergence and outperform the untuned base model with CoT instructions. In both teacher settings, SFT+DisCorD is the strongest distilled method, which improves over SFT by 3.0 and 2.0 points, respectively. Consistent with Section 5.2, adding DisCorD also improves the symmetric-KL objective in both settings. These results suggest that the proposed mismatch-aware reweighting remains effective across different distillation settings.

5.4 Distribution Divergence Measurement

To evaluate reasoning robustness under student-generated prefixes, we sampled prefixes from the base student before training instead of from teacher traces. Specifically, we randomly sampled 200 MATH test problems and let the base student model generate partial solutions. From each partial solution, we truncated prefix horizons with t∈{32,64,128,256}t\in\{32,64,128,256\} tokens. Figure 2 reports ExAccErr (↓\downarrow) for SFT and our method, where lower values indicate smaller divergence between the student model’s continuation answers and the expected answer distribution under the given prefixes. Specifically, each continuation answer is sampled from the trained student model conditioned on a provided prefix.

As the prefix horizon tt increases, SFT exhibits a notably growing ExAccErr, which indicates that its behavior becomes increasingly unstable when conditioned on longer student-generated reasoning prefixes. In contrast, DisCorD keeps ExAccErr stable across prefix lengths. This indicates that our proposed distribution correction improves robustness to prefix drift and reduces the amplification of errors introduced by student-generated intermediate reasoning. Overall, this result shows that the benefit of DisCorD is not limited to final-answer accuracy. By reducing sensitivity to long student-generated prefixes, it better preserves reliable continuation behavior within support regions likely to be visited by student models.

5.5 Reasoning Quality Analysis

In addition to the improved final-answer accuracy and reduced teacher-student distribution drift as shown above, we examined whether performance gains of our method manifest in the generated reasoning traces themselves. In particular, we investigated whether the correct answers are supported by more logically coherent and stable reasoning traces, and whether reducing the distribution drift in training alleviates typical generation failures such as repetition, post-answer continuation (i.e., non-stop generation after providing a final answer), and inconsistent final answers (i.e., providing multiple distinct answers). For fair comparisons, we focused primarily on commonly-correct examples where both SFT and DisCorD produce the correct final answer.

Reasoning Trace Pattern Quality.

To examine whether our method improves generation patterns, we compared DisCorD with the SFT baseline using four automatic trace-quality metrics: mean trace length in characters (Mean len), the fraction of repeated 4-grams in the generated trace (Rep. 4-gram), the rate of continuing generation after emitting a final answer (Post-answer), and the rate of producing multiple distinct final-answer statements within the same trace (Multi-answer). As shown in Table 4, on MATH, our method decreases the mean trace length from 4383.0 to 1357.9 characters and the multiple-answer rate from 0.75 to 0, while also substantially lowering repetition and post-answer continuation rates. A similar pattern also appears on OlympiadBench. Beyond improving final-answer accuracy, even within the commonly correct subset, DisCorD yields cleaner generation patterns by producing shorter traces with fewer repetitions, post-answer continuations, and multiple-answer failures.

Evaluation of Reasoning Trace Quality.

To complement the automatic metrics above, we further evaluated the generated traces using GPT-5.4 mini as a judge with a predefined rubric. The rubric covers five dimensions: cleanliness, validity (i.e., whether the reasoning is valid when the answer is correct), self-consistency, reasoning quality, and verification quality. Appendix D provides the definitions of each metric, the scoring protocol, and the full results. As shown in Figure 3, these AI-as-judge annotation results are consistent with the evaluation using automatic metrics in Table 4. Crucially, this suggests that the shorter responses produced by DisCorD are not merely more concise but also more logically coherent and internally consistent. The detailed results further show that DisCorD reduces the fraction of traces with a correct final answer but flawed reasoning from 26% to 11% on OlympiadBench and from 20% to 7% on MATH. In addition, DisCorD receives higher reasoning and verification quality scores. These results together indicate a qualitative improvement in the reasoning traces underlying the final-answer accuracy gains.

Reasoning Trace Case Study.

We further analyzed representative examples from one in-domain dataset, MATH, and one out-of-domain dataset, OlympiadBench. A concise case summary and representative trace analyses are provided in Appendix I. The examples illustrate two qualitative patterns. (1) First, in failure-recovery cases, where DisCorD answers correctly while the SFT baseline fails (example A–D), our method more reliably preserves the underlying reasoning structure of the teacher solution, even when it does not exactly reproduce the teacher’s surface-level formatting, such as the section headers: “PLAN”, “VERIFICATION”, etc. Specifically, in the OlympiadBench divisor-counting problem, DisCorD does not verbatim reproduce the teacher’s verification section titled "VEriFICATION", but it keeps the teacher’s core logic by using the correct factorization and checks the resulting answer consistently. In contrast, the SFT baseline follows the expected template more closely, but its verification step uses an incorrect factorization and counting argument that leads to the wrong answer. (2) Second, in overlap-correct cases (example E–H), where both models reach the correct final answer, DisCorD often produces a cleaner and more direct solution, with fewer unnecessary branches and more relevant checks. These observations are consistent with the aforementioned metrics: DisCorD can improve reasoning trace reliability by preserving core reasoning content instead of verbatim imitating the teacher’s formatting.

Overall, our qualitative studies indicate that DisCorD improves reasoning trace reliability beyond final-answer accuracy. On commonly correct examples, our method yields cleaner and more logically stable traces; in failure-recovery cases, it more often preserves the mathematical structure needed to reach the correct answer. These findings imply that student-support-aware distribution correction strengthens offline reasoning distillation not by enforcing surface-level template imitation, but by reallocating teacher supervision toward reasoning behaviors that the student can more reliably carry through at inference time.

5.6 Comparing Alternative Correction-Weight Designs

Table 5 compares several correction-weight designs under the same prompt and evaluation setting. The rows evaluate our proposed weighting from Eq. (7) against clipped exponential weighting, the raw log-ratio, and a one-sided ReLU transform. Our formulation achieves the strongest result among the tested variants and inherits a theoretical interpretation grounded in noise-contrastive estimation.

6 Conclusion and Future Work

We propose a simple yet effective offline distillation method for mitigating teacher–student distribution drift in tasks requiring long reasoning traces. Our method keeps the training data fully offline but reweights teacher-token supervision based on a student–teacher support ratio, thereby prioritizing teacher behaviors that are more compatible with the student’s inference-time distribution. Comprehensive evaluation on mathematical reasoning benchmarks shows that our method improves final-answer accuracy over strong offline baselines, narrows the gap to online student-rollout distillation, and yields more logical and higher-quality reasoning traces. While our experiments focus on mathematical reasoning, the proposed method can be extended to other long-horizon generation settings, including code generation, scientific reasoning, and tool-use agents. Future work may include integrating our method with off-policy or online training to better balance data efficiency and distillation efficacy. Another future direction is to decouple teacher trace generation from distribution correction scoring: when a trace-generating teacher is unavailable or unknown, a proxy reference model—potentially a weaker one—or an arbitrary policy may be used to approximate the support-ratio weights. This may preserve the core benefit of prioritizing student-reachable tokens while offering greater flexibility in the trade-off between teacher data quality and robustness to training-inference distribution shift.

Appendix

Appendix A DisCorD Temperature Tuning

Table A reports the sigmoid temperatures used for the DisCORD-augmented rows in the main result tables. We tune this temperature within each teacher–student setting and base objective, rather than using a single global value across all experiments. This is because the scale of the student–teacher log-probability gap can change with teacher size, student capacity, dataset, and whether DisCORD is applied on top of SFT or symmetric KL. For MATH-trained checkpoints, the same temperature is used for the MATH500 in-domain evaluation and for the OOD evaluations, since the OOD benchmarks reuse the MATH-trained models. GSM8K results are listed separately because they come from independently trained GSM8K checkpoints.

Appendix B Teacher Chain-of-Thought Prompt

We designed this teacher CoT prompt ourselves to elicit structured, self-verifying reasoning with explicit understanding, strategy, solution, and verification stages. Following established prompt design principles such as role specification, explicit output structure, and self-consistency checks [39, 37], we refined the template on a held-out sample of training questions and did not tune the prompt against the evaluation benchmarks.

Appendix C Training and Evaluation Audit Details

This section collects the implementation details used to make the experimental comparisons auditable. The main comparison is objective-level: within each teacher–student–dataset setting, all offline objectives are trained on the same retained teacher-generated trace corpus and differ only in the loss or token weighting applied to that corpus.

Training corpus construction.

For MATH-family experiments, teacher traces are generated from the MATH training split (7,5007{,}500 source problems). For GSM8K experiments, teacher traces are generated from the GSM8K training split (7,4737{,}473 source problems). Each source problem is prompted once with the structured teacher prompt in Appendix B; the generated trace is then filtered by the same final-answer equivalence judge used in evaluation. We retain only teacher-correct traces for distillation. The retained subset, retained count, and average teacher-trace length are fixed before student training and are shared by all offline objectives within the corresponding teacher–student setting. Cross-family Llama experiments reuse the same Qwen2.5 teacher-trace construction pipeline as the Qwen-student experiments.

Offline Training Protocol and hyperparameters.

Within a teacher–student setting and data split, the fully offline methods (SFT, KL, symmetric KL, ToDi, and DisCorD-augmented variants) are trained on the same retained teacher-correct examples and use the same offline training recipe: AdamW with learning rate 3×10−63\times 10^{-6}, weight decay 0.010.01, cosine decay with 5%5\% warmup, gradient clipping at norm 1.01.0, bfloat16 mixed precision, maximum sequence length 2048, random seed 42, and effective batch size 16. For MATH-family runs, this corresponds to micro-batch size 1 with gradient accumulation 16; for GSM8K, micro-batch size 2 with gradient accumulation 8. The number of epochs is fixed within each matched setting and base objective, so changes in Table 1, Table 2, and Table 3 are not attributable to different amounts of offline teacher data or different offline training-token budgets. Hyperparameters that define an objective itself, such as the KL/ToDi temperature or the sigmoid temperature for DisCorD, are selected per setting and base objective and are reported in the corresponding table captions or rows when they differ.

Online Protocol and hyperparameters.

GKD is reported separately because it is not a compute-matched offline baseline. It uses student rollouts during training and follows its own on-policy recipe: AdamW with learning rate 3×10−63\times 10^{-6}, weight decay 0.010.01, cosine decay with 5%5\% warmup, gradient clipping at norm 1.01.0, maximum sequence length 2048, effective batch size 16, β=0.5\beta=0.5 following the original paper setting, and one training epoch in the reported runs, with the on-policy mixing parameter λ\lambda specified by the corresponding run. We therefore treat GKD as an online reference rather than as evidence about the matched offline training-token budget.

Evaluation protocol.

All methods in a setting use the same evaluation prompt, greedy decoding protocol, and maximum generation length. The generation caps are 2048 new tokens for GSM8K, MATH500, and 4096 new tokens for AMC23, Omni-Math and OlympiadBench. Final-answer correctness is judged by GPT-5.4-mini using the same mathematical-equivalence prompt for every method. The judge is not given the method identity and is instructed to ignore reasoning quality and compare only the final answer. If a solution contains multiple candidate answers, the judge follows the explicitly marked final answer, such as one introduced by “final”, “answer”, “therefore”, or \boxed{}. The full judge prompt appears in Appendix D.

Compute resources.

Experiments were run on SLURM-managed GPU clusters. Unless otherwise noted, training and evaluation jobs used NVIDIA A100 40GB GPUs; GPU-hours are reported as the number of allocated GPUs multiplied by wall-clock runtime. In the main 7B→\rightarrow3B comparison, the DisCorD run uses no online student-rollout tokens and requires 3.12 GPU-hours, whereas the GKD online baseline generates about 2.86M student-rollout tokens and requires 49.56 GPU-hours. The reported GPU-hour comparison covers training compute for the matched distillation setting; teacher-trace generation, benchmark evaluation, and GPT-5.4-mini judge calls are one-time preprocessing or evaluation costs shared across methods within each setting.

Appendix D Evaluation Details and Correctness Judge

Main in-domain evaluation uses MATH500 [20] for MATH-trained checkpoints (n=500n=500) and GSM8K [6] for GSM8K-trained checkpoints (n=1,319n=1{,}319). OOD evaluation uses the non-combinatorics portion of OlympiadBench OE_TO_maths_en_COMP (n=520n=520 after removing combinatorics problems), the fixed Omni-Math D3/D4 paper subset [8] (n=200n=200), and AMC23 (n=40n=40). We exclude OlympiadBench combinatorics problems because the MATH teacher-trace training corpus used here contains no combinatorics examples.

All distilled checkpoints are evaluated with the same finetuning-style prompt template and greedy decoding. We use generation caps of 2048 new tokens for GSM8K, MATH500, and AMC23, and 4096 new tokens for Omni-Math and OlympiadBench.

Appendix G DisCorD Applied to KL Distillation Objective

For KL-based offline distillation, we apply the same token-level sigmoid correction used in Eq. (5) to the teacher–student next-token divergence. The corresponding loss is

ℒKL+DisCorD(θ)=𝔼x∼𝒬,y∼πT(⋅∣x;c)[∑trt𝒟KL(π¯T(⋅∣x,y<t;c)∥πθ(⋅∣x,y<t))],\mathcal{L}^{\mathrm{KL}+\textsc{DisCorD}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{Q},\;y\sim\pi_{T}(\cdot\mid x;c)}\left[\sum_{t}r_{t}\,\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\bar{\pi}_{T}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t};c)\,\middle\|\,\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t})\right)\right], (6)

where

rt=σ⁡(τ​log⁡π¯θ​(yt∣x,y<t)π¯T​(yt∣x,y<t;c)).r_{t}=\sigma\!\left(\tau\log\frac{\bar{\pi}_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})}{\bar{\pi}_{T}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t};c)}\right). (7)

Here π¯\bar{\pi} denotes a stop-gradient distribution and τ\tau is the sigmoid temperature.

Appendix H Definition of ExAccErr Metric

We follow the original MiniLLM-style ExAccErr definition. For an input question xx, let yT=(y1T,…,yTT)y^{T}=(y^{T}_{1},\ldots,y^{T}_{T}) denote the teacher CoT rollout and let ym=(y1m,…,yTmm)y^{m}=(y^{m}_{1},\ldots,y^{m}_{T_{m}}) denote the rollout of method m∈{SFT,Ours}m\in\{\text{SFT},\text{Ours}\}. At step tt, given a prefix z<tz_{<t}, we define the teacher–student next-token gap as

dtm(z<t)=KL(pT(⋅∣x,z<t)∥qm(⋅∣x,z<t)),d_{t}^{m}(z_{<t})=\mathrm{KL}\!\left(p_{T}(\cdot\mid x,z_{<t})\,\|\,q_{m}(\cdot\mid x,z_{<t})\right),

where pTp_{T} and qmq_{m} are the teacher and method-mm student next-token distributions, respectively. We then accumulate this gap under teacher prefixes and under method-mm student prefixes:

Eteacherm​(ℓ)=∑t=1ℓdtm​(y<tT),Estudentm​(ℓ)=∑t=1ℓdtm​(y<tm),E_{\mathrm{teacher}}^{m}(\ell)=\sum_{t=1}^{\ell}d_{t}^{m}(y^{T}_{<t}),\qquad E_{\mathrm{student}}^{m}(\ell)=\sum_{t=1}^{\ell}d_{t}^{m}(y^{m}_{<t}),

and define

ExAccErrm​(ℓ)=Estudentm​(ℓ)−Eteacherm​(ℓ)Eteacherm​(ℓ)×100%.\mathrm{ExAccErr}^{m}(\ell)=\frac{E_{\mathrm{student}}^{m}(\ell)-E_{\mathrm{teacher}}^{m}(\ell)}{E_{\mathrm{teacher}}^{m}(\ell)}\times 100\%.

Lower metrics are desirable.

Appendix I Reasoning Trace Case Study

Table I summarizes the eight qualitative examples discussed in Section 5.5. Examples A–D are failure-recovery cases, where DisCorD reaches the correct final answer while the SFT baseline fails. Examples E–H are overlap-correct cases, where both student models answer correctly and the comparison focuses on trace quality. To keep the appendix concise, we summarize all eight cases and reproduce the original raw traces for two representative cases only.

The problem asks for the greatest prime factor of the divisor count of 20T​23T20^{T}23^{T} with T=21T=21. The teacher’s core solution is 20T​23T=22​T​5T​23T20^{T}23^{T}=2^{2T}5^{T}23^{T} and K=(2​T+1)​(T+1)2=43⋅222K=(2T+1)(T+1)^{2}=43\cdot 22^{2}. DisCorD preserves this divisor-count factorization and identifies 43. SFT follows the surface template more closely, but its verification incorrectly factors 2081220812 as 22⋅7⋅7432^{2}\cdot 7\cdot 743 and therefore changes the answer to 743. This shows that DisCorD need not copy the teacher’s headings to retain the mathematical structure that matters.
